An idea worked out in a Hyde Park seminar room had been turned into a national machine.
And while the federal government drew its lines, private owners built their own.
The favorite tool was the racially restrictive covenant, a clause written into a deed promising that the property would never be sold or rented to Black residents, and sometimes to Asians or Jews.

In Chicago whole subdivisions signed them, block clubs went door to door collecting names, and the University of Chicago itself quietly bankrolled the defense of covenants in the neighborhoods around its campus.
From 1933 to 1947 the University spent more than eighty three thousand dollars protecting them.
The covenant and the redline worked as a pair.
The other kept the people out.
Together they held the South Side Black Belt in place like a clamp.
Which brings us back to one block.
In the spring of 1937 a Black real estate broker named Carl Hansberry bought a three flat at 6140 South Rhodes Avenue, just south of Washington Park.
